problem: WaveScheduler.Tick appends one SpawnRequest to the caller's buffer for every spawn interval that elapsed during dt, with no ceiling. For a normal frame this is zero or one. For a large dt it is dt divided by the spawn interval: at the sim's own configuration of SpawnInterval 2f (Studio/sim/MergeSurvivor.Sim/Program.cs:29), a dt of 1e6 seconds appends five hundred thousand requests in a single call, and a dt just below the point where the schedule can no longer advance appends on the order of sixteen million. This is finite, defined and deterministic -- it is not the CHA-0001 non-termination defect, which is separately remedied under WO-0010 per RUL-0003 -- but for an unattended harness the practical outcome of a sixteen-million-item append is the same night's work lost. The remedy ruled in RUL-0003 removes non-termination and deliberately does not touch this: it makes the extreme end of the dt range throw rather than hang, and leaves the middle of the range allocating without bound. That is the correct division of labour, because capping catch-up is a decision about what a long hitch should produce for a player -- design's call, not engineering's, quality's or mine. The question has been logged twice now (PRO-0006 notes, and RUL-0002's non-blocking list) and never routed to the division that owns it. Logging it a third time is not a decision.
evidence: Assets/Core/Spawning/WaveScheduler.cs:70-75 -- the loop appends one SpawnRequest per elapsed interval with no ceiling on the count; the class comment at lines 7-13 documents carrying the remainder across ticks as deliberate behaviour, so the absence of a cap is a design position and not an oversight.

Studio/sim/MergeSurvivor.Sim/Program.cs:29 and 224-239 -- SpawnInterval is 2f and RunSchedule takes dt as a parameter chosen by the caller. Today only 1f/30f, 1f/60f and 1f/240f are used, so nothing hits this now; the harness is the component that legitimately chooses its own dt and the one that runs unattended.

Studio/state/proposals/PRO-0006.json, notes (b) -- qa-director derived this limit, judged correctly that capping is a design decision rather than a defect for engineering to fix unasked, and logged it rather than inflating it into work. This proposal routes that finding; it does not re-derive it.
Studio/state/rulings/RUL-0003.json, matter 6 -- the CHA-0001 remedy fixes non-termination and explicitly not unbounded allocation, and records the interaction between the two.

Assets/Unity/EnemySpawner.cs:45 -- the shipped shell passes Time.deltaTime, so no realistic frame reaches a count above single digits. This is a harness and tooling concern, not a player-facing one, and should not be prioritised as though it were.
proposedWork: A decision from the game designer, not an engineering order, and the decision is the deliverable. The question: should WaveScheduler emit at most N spawn requests from a single Tick call, and if so what is N and what happens to the surplus -- discarded, or retained in the timer so it emerges over subsequent ticks? Any N large enough to be unreachable in play (a five-second hitch at interval 2f produces three spawns) and small enough to bound allocation (a few thousand) is invisible to players and to every existing test, so the design risk is low; but the choice of semantics for the surplus is genuinely a design choice about whether a stalled client owes the player the content it missed. If design answers 'no ceiling, catch-up is the point', that is a legitimate answer, should be recorded as such, and this proposal closes with the limit documented in the class comment so nobody re-derives it a fourth time. If design answers with a ceiling, an L3 engineering order follows, scoped to Assets/Core/Spawning/** and Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/**, with a regression test that a very large accepted dt returns exactly N and appends exactly N items. Sequencing constraint: this must not be dispatched against WaveScheduler.cs until the CHA-0001 remedy under WO-0010 is merged and gated, per RUL-0003 matter 5. Authorisation limit, stated so it is not assumed: a ceiling would subsume the CHA-0001 remedy's rejection contract, and replacing that remedy's ratchet assertion (Tick(1e8f) throws) with a ceiling assertion (Tick(1e8f) returns N) is the replacement of a passing assertion and requires written authorisation under L-002 at that time. RUL-0003 does not grant it in advance and neither does this proposal.
expectedBenefit: Puts a question that has now been logged three times to the only division that can answer it, and gets either a bounded allocation or an explicit, recorded design position that unbounded catch-up is intended. Either outcome ends the re-derivation. The second-order benefit is the one I care about more: it keeps the CHA-0001 remedy narrow. Bundling a behaviour decision into a correctness fix is what would have made that remedy risky, and routing the behaviour decision separately is what lets the correctness fix be provably behaviour-preserving.
notes: Deliberately NOT proposed here, to keep the question answerable in one sitting. (a) Whether the harness itself should defend against absurd dt at its own call sites rather than relying on Core to reject them. Core rejecting inputs it cannot process is the right layer and the CHA-0001 remedy provides it; a second guard in Program.cs would be belt and braces on a component with no players. (b) Whether SpawnRequest should be a struct emitted into a pooled buffer rather than appended to an IList. That is an allocation-shape question for engineering, is orthogonal to whether a ceiling exists, and would confuse this decision if attached to it.
